penalties_applied.name: requires_human_fulfillment
penalties_applied.reason: Onboarding each author requires collecting, curating, and licensing their content (books, talks, interviews), which is per-customer manual work that cannot be automated.

penalties_applied.name: requires_synchronous_human
penalties_applied.reason: Signing authors as 'licensors' requires negotiation, contract review, and relationship management — inherently synchronous and human-intensive.

rationale: The concept is intellectually interesting but commercially fragile for a solo operator. The buyer picture is split and weak: readers (B2C) rarely pay $15 per book for a chat interface when free summaries exist, and authors/publishers (B2B) need active relationship sales plus legal licensing agreements before anything can be built. Operational autonomy is low because every author onboarding is bespoke — content must be licensed, curated, and validated per author, which is non-automatable manual work. The total collapses to 2.1 after applying the human-fulfillment and synchronous-human penalties, which accurately reflect the sales-call and content-licensing reality. Drop and monitor; revisit if a major publisher signals intent to license at scale.
solution_plan: This opportunity is not viable for a solo non-technical operator using this factory. The core bottleneck is supply-side: every author requires a licensing agreement and content ingestion before any reader can use the product. That is per-customer legal and relationship work that Claude cannot automate. The demand side is also unproven — $15/book is a high bar when readers can get free AI book summaries. There is no realistic path to hands-off operation here. Do not build.
notes: Total falls to 2.1 after penalties — well below min_total_to_validate (5.5). Primary issues: buyer_clarity=4 (split B2C/B2B with no clear high-budget buyer), operational_autonomy=4 (per-author content licensing is manual), and penalties for human fulfillment and synchronous sales work.
